reference.source: GeneReviews mitochondrial DNA depletion / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: This is a group of autosomal recessive nuclear disorders in which the amount, rather than the sequence, of mitochondrial DNA is reduced in affected tissues
They are broadly grouped by phenotype into myopathic (for example TK2), encephalomyopathic (for example SUCLA2, RRM2B), hepatocerebral (for example DGUOK, MPV17, POLG) and neurogastrointestinal forms
Causative genes maintain the mitochondrial nucleotide pool or replicate mitochondrial DNA, so their failure starves post-mitotic tissues of intact mitochondrial genomes
Because inheritance is Mendelian and nuclear, recurrence risk follows autosomal recessive expectations rather than the maternal transmission seen with primary mitochondrial DNA mutations
Hepatocerebral forms present in infancy with liver failure and neurological features, while myopathic forms present with progressive weakness and hypotonia
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number in affected tissue alongside targeted or panel nuclear gene testing
Sodium valproate is avoided where POLG or a hepatocerebral depletion disorder is suspected because of hepatotoxicity risk, and care is otherwise supportive
reference.pathophysiology: Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes are caused by recessive mutations in nuclear genes that either supply the deoxyribonucleotide building blocks for mitochondrial DNA (such as TK2, DGUOK, SUCLA2, SUCLG1 and RRM2B), maintain the mitochondrial environment (such as MPV17), or replicate the genome directly (POLG, TWNK). Impairment of any of these functions reduces the number of intact mitochondrial genomes per cell, and because mitochondrial DNA encodes essential respiratory-chain subunits, oxidative phosphorylation fails in a tissue-specific pattern that reflects each gene's expression and each tissue's energy demand. Post-mitotic, energy-hungry tissues such as muscle, brain and liver are most vulnerable, giving the myopathic, encephalomyopathic and hepatocerebral phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Primary mitochondrial DNA point mutation or deletion syndromes
Spinal muscular atrophy and congenital myopathies (for myopathic forms)
Neonatal haemochromatosis and other infantile liver failure syndromes
Glycogen storage and fatty acid oxidation disorders
additionalInvestigations: Quantification of mitochondrial DNA copy number in muscle or liver
Nuclear gene panel or exome sequencing covering TK2, DGUOK, MPV17, SUCLA2, RRM2B, POLG and related genes
Respiratory-chain enzyme assays in affected tissue showing combined complex deficiencies
Liver function and coagulation studies in hepatocerebral presentations
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids (for example methylmalonic aciduria in SUCLA2/SUCLG1 defects)
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory muscle involvement
Metabolic decompensation with severe lactic acidosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by subtype and gene: severe infantile hepatocerebral and encephalomyopathic forms often carry a poor outlook with early mortality, whereas some myopathic forms are more slowly progressive, and outcome depends heavily on the specific genetic defect and organ involvement.
pitfalls: Confusing these nuclear, Mendelian disorders with maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA diseases when counselling families
Failing to sample the clinically affected tissue, so depletion is missed in blood
Administering valproate in POLG or hepatocerebral forms and precipitating liver failure
Not recognising specific biochemical clues such as mild methylmalonic aciduria pointing to SUCLA2 or SUCLG1 defects
management: No universal cure, but TK2 deficiency has disease-specific nucleoside substrate therapy using deoxycytidine and deoxythymidine (pyrimidine nucleoside) supplementation that can improve the myopathic phenotype
Supportive mitochondrial cofactor supplementation, nutritional support and avoidance of fasting and catabolic stress
Avoid mitochondrial toxins, especially sodium valproate in POLG-related disease
Phenotype-directed care: ventilatory and physiotherapy support for myopathic weakness, management of liver failure in hepatocerebral forms, and anticonvulsants for encephalomyopathic seizures
Treat metabolic decompensation and lactic acidosis with intravenous dextrose and fluids
Surveillance of respiratory function, cardiac status, growth and neurodevelopment across the subtypes
Multidisciplinary care with autosomal recessive genetic counselling and prenatal and carrier testing
